versions.analysis_for_next:
Version 0 scored 70.9 macro-F1. Neutral is the weak class: 52 of 108 gold-neutral tweets were mislabelled, split evenly between positive (26) and negative (26). The model also sent 15 gold-negative tweets to neutral.

Patterns in the errors:
1. News headlines. Annotators seem to label many headlines by the valence of the reported event, despite the v0 instruction to ignore that.
   - Negative: a budget deficit, a missile strike, a bail ruling, a funeral, a phone that may break, an eviction stirring bad feelings.
   - Positive: a tennis win, a UFC title, a historic Mass, a 'delighted' celebrity.
   - The model called most of these neutral. I will drop the 'not good or bad news' clause. Instead, clearly good or bad reported events take that label, and routine or ambiguous news stays neutral.
2. Neutral predicted positive. These include plain event announcements and promotions (trunk show, info morning, charity walk, radio show, ministry meetup), fan requests, plans to go to a game or film, and sports play-by-play. I will require explicit enthusiasm or praise for positive. Plain logistics or promotion becomes neutral even when the event sounds fun.
3. Neutral predicted negative. These include light self-deprecating grumbles with 'lol', 'lmao' or 'I'm dead', playful dread ('not ready for this album'), wry sports or political banter, and minor mishaps.
   - Negative should need real disappointment, anger, sadness or pointed criticism.
   - Light, joking or mixed grumbles become neutral.
   - This partly reverses the v0 rule that humor never rescues a complaint. I will keep negative for genuine complaints, cancelled plans that clearly upset the author, and hostile insults.
4. Some sarcasm and argumentative replies remain noisy. I will keep the sarcasm cue and add that argumentative replies rebutting someone lean negative.

The gold labels look noisy, so I am aiming at the bulk of these patterns rather than individual tweets.

Version 1 raised macro-F1 to 72.2, but it overcorrected toward neutral. Positive recall fell from 89 to 72, and 33 gold-positive tweets went to neutral.

Main gold-positive misses:
- Upbeat invitations and promotions: 'come join', 'come support', 'free scoop', 'win a car', 'get your tickets', ticket giveaways, an internship info session, a 99-cent 'thank you gift'.
- Mild personal enjoyment or plans for fun things: 'perfect Friday night', rereading a favourite book, 'I will celebrate all day', 'for sure going to watch', 'fast forward to the concert', Bee Gees on loop.
- Hopes and prayers.
- Friendly encouragement ('Get it :-)').

The remaining neutral-to-positive errors include:
- Dry news.
- Sports results without author emotion.
- Fan requests ('we want you to...', 'please sing at my wedding').
- Purely logistical notices.

Plan for positive vs neutral: positive if the author invites, hypes or offers something fun, free or exciting, or shows any enjoyment, hope or anticipation. Neutral if the tweet is purely logistical or reportorial.

Negative vs neutral is balanced at 19/19. Gold-negative misses that went to neutral:
- Personal dread or self-deprecation ('going to die', 'no talent', not enjoying, 'Desperation Day', bad food).
- Pointed questions criticising politicians or groups.

Many neutrals predicted negative are wry sports or political commentary and joking mishaps. So personal unhappiness, even phrased jokingly, stays negative. Detached wry commentary about public figures, teams or companies without clear hostility becomes neutral.

I will drop 'lol softens to neutral' for first-person complaints. I will keep the news-valence rule but require a clearly good or bad event.

Version 2 overcorrected toward positive and negative. Neutral recall collapsed to 43/108: 36 neutrals went to positive and 29 to negative, and macro-F1 fell to 69.6. Version 1 (72.2) remains the best base, but it lost too much positive recall.

I will rebuild from v1 with targeted positive additions and firmer neutral guards.

1. Neutrals that v2 called positive:
   - Plain event notices (trunk show, ministry meetup, info morning, radio show).
   - Spam-like free offers.
   - Fan pleas.
   - Flat plans ('going to the game Friday').
   - Speculative news ('may be positioning').
   - Mild opinions on TV and politics.
   - Sports updates.
   These should stay neutral unless the author expresses explicit feeling words or hype.
2. Positives that v1 missed:
   - Explicit enjoyment ('perfect night', 'celebrate all day').
   - Hopes, prayers and RIP condolences. v2 even sent some condolences to negative, so they need an explicit statement.
   - Upbeat invitations with prizes or giveaways plus excitement markers.
3. Neutrals that v2 called negative:
   - Hyperbolic jokes ('I'm dead', 'lmao', 'not ready', 'Nooo').
   - Wry sports and political commentary.
   - Small mishaps.
   - Headlines with a negative word but no clearly bad event.
   v1's handling of these worked better, so I restore it.

I will add a decision rule: neutral is the default for informational, logistical, speculative or joking content. Positive or negative needs an explicit feeling or a clearly good or bad event.

Version 3 is the best so far at 73.3. Neutral recall is good (85/108), but neutral now absorbs too much: 31 positives and 28 negatives went to neutral. The v3 negative criterion was also truncated in my output, which probably cost negative recall (75/108). The fix is to restore a full negative definition and to widen positive and negative carefully, keeping the neutral guards that worked.

Positive misses mostly fall into three groups:
- First-person anticipation of attending something fun: 'this time tomorrow I'll be at...!', 'fast forward to the concert', 'for sure going to watch', 'come with us!!'.
- Invitations or promotions for the author's own or a featured event, with calls to action and exclamation: 'come support', 'Get your tickets now!', 'Please Share!!!', ticket giveaways, 'interested in interning?'.
- Light personal enjoyment or favourable predictions: rereading a favourite book, Bee Gees on loop, 'has a good chance of winning', defending someone.

Negative misses are mostly calm or implicit criticism:
- Political or social critique and skeptical rhetorical questions: 'was he speaking TO cameras?', 'why did they bomb?', 'why haven't they put...'.
- Judgmental remarks: 'insensitive', 'yellow journalism', 'judging you', 'Desperation Day', 'TAKS on steroids'.
- Mockery of appearance and sarcasm.
- Personal dread: 'going to die', 'no talent', 'NOOOO'.
- Headlines reporting a defect, injury, bail for a militant, or a deficit.

The neutral-to-negative errors that remain are mostly self-deprecating jokes about trivial mishaps and wry sports quips. I will keep those as neutral.

Version 4 scored 73.5, essentially tied with v3 (73.3). Positive recall (94) and negative recall (98) are strong, but neutral recall collapsed to 51/108: 32 neutrals went to positive and 25 to negative. v3 had the opposite balance, with neutral at 85 but positive at 76 and negative at 75. The goal for v5 is to keep v4's positive and negative definitions and add explicit neutral carve-outs that take priority, so that only the recurring false-positive and false-negative types move back to neutral.

Neutral tweets that v4 called positive:
- Community or organizational notices: 'come along', 'sign up', 'register', 'RSVP', 'meeting this Sunday', radio show listings, interview links.
- Fan pleas and requests to celebrities ('please sing at my wedding', 'we want you to come').
- Sports scores and play-by-play stated without the author's own excitement.
- Speculative or soft-news headlines (a study says fears 'may not come to pass', a company 'may be positioning', a royal birthday, a celebrity birth).
- Mild comparative opinions on TV or politics.
- Trivia and casual plans ('X sounds like the move').

Neutral tweets that v4 called negative:
- Wry quips about athletes, games, films and companies.
- Self-deprecating jokes about trivial personal mishaps.
- News with a loaded word ('tirade', 'apologises', 'worst offense') but no clear harm.

Genuine criticism of politicians or serious issues, personal dread, and clearly bad news remain negative.

Version 5 is the best so far at 76.5, with balanced recall (positive 86, neutral 69, negative 94). The remaining errors are scattered and many look like label noise, such as sarcastic positives and literal-looking negatives. I will make small, targeted edits and keep the v5 structure.

1. Positive misses:
   - Celebratory holiday or treat promotions ('Come celebrate with a free scoop', 'meet us for a delicious lunch treat'). v5's notice carve-out swallowed these.
   - Eager personal plans ('for sure going to watch').
   - Playful encouragement ('Get it :-)').
   I will add these to positive and make clear that the notice carve-out covers only dry informational or organizational notices.
2. Neutral predicted positive:
   - Sports results and live updates (a seed advancing, an upset in progress).
   - Weather reports.
   - Mild TV and political opinions.
   - Trivia.
   I will reinforce that results and live updates are neutral unless the author states their own happiness, and add weather and soft facts.
3. Neutral predicted negative:
   - Teasing quips about athletes' or teams' performance (implode, pitching staff, 'could be worse'), still miscalled despite the carve-out.
   - Self-deprecating mishap jokes.
   I will make the sports-teasing carve-out explicit. Political criticism and personal sadness stay negative, since these mostly score correctly.

Version 6 is the best so far at 77.5. Its sports carve-out over-applied, though. Major results with positive gold labels went to neutral: Serena continuing her Grand Slam march, McGregor winning a title, and Federer reaching a final. A gold-neutral early-round advance by a 15th seed, which v5 had wrongly called positive, no longer appears among the errors. I will refine the rule: titles, finals, championships, records and big milestones are positive, while routine or early-round results and in-progress scores are neutral.

Neutral-to-negative errors (25) are now the largest bucket. Two clusters recur:
- Snarky asides on shared news or about public figures and companies, such as an ironic 'is forgiven', 'clear as mud', 'bad reputation', 'Bwahahaha' and 'NEVER!!!'. Annotators treat these punchy commentary tweets as neutral.
- Minor personal inconveniences and scheduling clashes framed jokingly or casually: long work shift 'lmao', a broken computer 'sorry', 'not ready', 'Nooo' about a clash, rapping instead of writing a paper.

I will sharpen both carve-outs. Negative will be reserved for serious criticism (policies, violence, ethics, insensitivity), clear personal unhappiness and bad-event news. I won't push further on gold negatives that are hard to detect; some, like the Halifax travel reply, look like noise.

Version 7 is the best so far at 78.7. Positive recall (94) and negative recall (93) are strong. The largest remaining bucket is neutral predicted as positive (23 tweets). Many of these already fall under existing carve-outs, but the model still leans positive, often with low confidence (0.50–0.60).

Recurring types among those 23:
- Soft celebrity or royal news: a birthday, a baby's birth, a picture doing well at the box office.
- Fan pleas and trending campaigns: 'we want you to...', 'please sing at my wedding', 'let's go trending'.
- Spammy 'free iPhone' offers.
- Plain trivia and stats (a rookie's ranking, who wrote lyrics, fight records).
- Speculative study headlines.
- Mild opinions about TV characters or candidates.
- Costume or attendance plans and 'X sounds like the move'.
- Radio or show listings, and a trunk show with RSVP.
- Live 'now watching' or score updates.

I will spell out these categories more concretely in the neutral carve-outs and stress that a plan or a fact is not positive without an explicit feeling word from the author. Everything that drives the current positive and negative recall stays unchanged.

Neutral-to-negative (16) is mostly snark on news and sports quips that are already covered. I will add 'loaded headline words' ('worst', 'tirade', 'apologises', 'bad reputation') to the soft-news carve-out, so that only clearly harmful events count as negative news.

Version 8 is the best so far at 79.3. Neutral predicted as positive fell to 14, but neutral predicted as negative rose to 23 and is now the largest bucket.

Most of those 23 already fall under existing carve-outs, yet the model often calls them negative with high confidence. I will tighten wording around three kinds of tweet.

1. Fandom or trivial hyperbole: 'I'm dead', 'not ready for this album', 'v sad' about missing a meet-up, 'Nooo' over a clash, rapping instead of writing a paper. These read as playful, not genuinely unhappy.
2. Punchline humor or snark about public figures, companies, sports performances and films: 'clear as mud', 'Bwahahaha', 'bad reputation', 'implode', 'pitching staff', 'not worth it'. These should stay neutral unless the target is a serious issue such as policy, violence, ethics or bigotry.
3. Headlines with loaded words but no concrete harm ('worst offense', 'is forgiven').

I will add a tie-break: when a tweet mixes humor with complaint about something trivial, choose neutral. Genuine personal disappointment ('disappointed', 'sucks', ':(' about real loss) and serious criticism stay negative, so negative recall should hold.

Positive and other criteria stay as they are, apart from light trimming.

Version 9 is the best so far at 79.8. Neutral recall is up to 77, but negative recall slipped from 94 to 89, and 13 gold negatives now go to neutral.

Those 13 include three kinds of tweet:
- Pointed but indirect political criticism: a skeptical question about a leader's sincerity on refugees, a remark on people who defended a hanged convict.
- Bitter self-deprecation about one's own worth or loneliness ('no talent', 'Desperation Day').
- Mockery of someone's appearance, and dismay interjections at news ('ACK').

The remaining neutral-to-negative errors (17) are snark on news and sports quips that the model resists reclassifying. Many errors look like label noise: sarcastic positives, a literal 'sick' meant as praise, and a travel reply labelled negative.

For this final version I will keep v9 almost intact. I will add a few precise negative cues for bitter self-deprecation, appearance mockery, dismay at news, and indirect criticism of politicians' sincerity. These are narrow enough that they shouldn't pull playful fandom hyperbole or celebrity snark out of neutral. I will also trim wording to stay under 300 words.
